conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one is here. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS—which looks at mood, anxiety, and overall emotional adjustment during the first postpartum year.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; it won’t go anywhere else without your permission. My goal is to create a calm, judgment-free space where you can answer honestly. There are just ten questions, and we’ll keep them conversational—no need to over-think, just tell me what feels true for you in the past seven days.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, when you were able to get a bit of rest, how did your sleep generally feel—did you fall asleep easily, wake a lot, or feel unrested even after a stretch of sleep?

Most nights I lie there for a long time—my mind just keeps spinning about whether the baby’s breathing okay, if I’ll hear her cry, if I’m doing everything right. I finally drift off, but then I jolt awake at every little sound or thought. When morning comes I feel like I never really slept, even if I technically got a few hours.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really... I mean, every now and then something small will make me crack a smile, but it fades fast. Mostly I feel like I’m stuck in a fog—nothing feels funny anymore, and when other people laugh I just feel more out of place.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little outings—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just taking the baby for a walk—but when the time comes, it feels flat, like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. I still go, and a part of me hopes it’ll feel fun, but the spark just isn’t really there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If she’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good-enough mom. Even little stuff, like the laundry piling up or forgetting to bring a burp cloth, spirals into “I’m failing at this.” I know in my head that’s not fair, but the guilt just shows up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. My heart races even when nothing’s happening—like when she’s napping peacefully I’ll suddenly worry she’s stopped breathing, or I’ll imagine dropping her when I stand up. There’s no real reason, but the fear just barges in and sits on my chest.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—sometimes it hits out of nowhere. My chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and suddenly I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even if everything around me is calm. It’s like my body’s sounding an alarm that I can’t turn off.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s another pile of dishes or laundry or a text I forgot to answer. I keep thinking, “How does everyone else manage?” Some mornings I just stare at the mess and feel like I can’t move. I do push through, but it’s like walking in wet cement.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… once she’s finally down and the house is quiet, my mind won’t shut up. I keep replaying every little thing I did wrong that day—did I hold her enough, did I snap at my partner, why didn’t I get the laundry folded—and the sadness just sits there. I’ll lie awake for an hour, sometimes two, before I drift off, and even then it’s light, jumpy sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day, at least for part of it. It’s like this gray cloud that follows me around—some hours are lighter, but the cloud never really lifts. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly feel tears in my throat for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, that’s been happening a few times this week. Nothing huge sets it off—sometimes it’s just looking at her and feeling like I’m already letting her down, or else I’ll catch sight of myself in the mirror and barely recognize the tired, puffy face staring back. I try to keep it quiet so the baby doesn’t pick up on it, but the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—no thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2–3 wks post-delivery  

**Chief Screening Findings**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, and daily tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding parenting competence (Q3)  
- Chronic, intrusive anxiety and episodic panic without clear precipitant (Q4, 5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and functional slowing (“walking in wet cement”) (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia linked to ruminative self-criticism (Q7)  

**Pattern Summary**  
Responses map strongly onto core criteria for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and co-occurring anxiety; symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, and cause subjective impairment in coping and enjoyment of motherhood.  

**Risk Factors**  
- Anhedonia, pervasive sadness, crying spells  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Excessive guilt / feelings of inadequacy as a mother  
- Spontaneous panic sensations  

**Safety**  
Denies any self-harm ideas (Q10); no current suicidal ideation reported.  

**Screening Conclusion**  
High clinical concern for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; further evaluation and possible referral for mental health follow-up recommended.
